Chapter 9: The Pushback—Tradition Fights Back
Not everyone’s ready to jump on board with this new way of thinking.
You can hear it in clubhouses, on talk radio, even in the sports columns—there’s no shortage of critics.
They’ll say baseball’s not just about numbers. The real magic? It’s in the unpredictable moments, the quirks, and, of course, the stories that make the game so human.
Some folks will even point to teams that flopped with analytics, or players who seem to defy every model, or those wild moments that just can’t be explained by a spreadsheet.
Inside the Athletics’ organization, you can feel the tension. Some of the veteran scouts are on edge, worried that all their years of experience are being pushed aside for algorithms and code.
They love the game, and they don’t want to see it boiled down to just a math problem.
On the other side, you’ve got analysts—folks who live and breathe data. Sometimes, they struggle to get their ideas across, or to connect with the scouts who trust their gut over a graph.
Picture this: one afternoon in the front office, a pretty heated argument kicks off. One scout swears up and down that a certain prospect just has “the look” of a star. But the analyst? He’s got a spreadsheet packed with red flags.
The general manager listens for a while, then asks a simple question: “What are we really trying to do here?”
Suddenly, the room goes quiet. In that stillness, it’s clear—the real goal isn’t about proving someone right. It’s about building the best team they possibly can.
Over time, both sides start to see the value in what the other brings. The scouts notice things you just can’t find in a data set—the way a player holds himself, or how he bounces back from a rough patch.
The analysts? They’re there to check for bias, to help cut through the noise and see what’s real.
The smartest decisions come when both perspectives are in the mix, when people listen to each other and work together.
Now, the pushback never really goes away. There’ll always be those who miss the old days, who believe some things just can’t be measured.
But the Athletics show something important—progress doesn’t mean throwing out tradition. It means building on it, finding new ways to honor the game you love.
